summary.text: Swapping the two square variables shows that \((a,b,c,d)\) is universal exactly when \((b,a,c,d)\) is, so any exact classification must be closed under exchanging its first two coordinates. But the proposed list contains \((1,2,1,1)\) and omits \((2,1,1,1)\), yielding a contradiction.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
U(a,b,c,d)
\]
denote the assertion that every natural number is representable in the form
\[
a x^2+b y^2+c z^3+d w^4
\]
with \(x,y,z,w\ge 0\). Thus
\[
U(a,b,c,d)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\forall n\in\mathbb N\;\exists x,y,z,w\in\mathbb N,
\quad a x^2+b y^2+c z^3+d w^4=n.
\]

The crucial observation is that universality is unchanged when the first two coefficients are interchanged:
\[
U(a,b,c,d)\Longleftrightarrow U(b,a,c,d).
\]
Indeed, suppose first that \(U(a,b,c,d)\) holds, and let \(n\) be any natural number. Choose nonnegative integers \(x,y,z,w\) such that
\[
a x^2+b y^2+c z^3+d w^4=n.
\]
For the form whose first two coefficients have been interchanged, take the new variables
\[
X=y,\qquad Y=x,\qquad Z=z,\qquad W=w.
\]
Then, using commutativity of addition,
\[
bX^2+aY^2+cZ^3+dW^4
=b y^2+a x^2+c z^3+d w^4
=a x^2+b y^2+c z^3+d w^4
=n.
\]
Since \(n\) was arbitrary, this proves \(U(b,a,c,d)\). Applying the same argument once more with \(a\) and \(b\) interchanged proves the reverse implication. This symmetry uses only the fact that both of the first two variables occur to the same power, namely the second power.

Now consider the two positive coefficient quadruples
\[
q=(1,2,1,1)
\quad\text{and}\quad
q'=(2,1,1,1).
\]
They are obtained from one another by interchanging the first two coefficients, so the symmetry just proved gives
\[
U(1,2,1,1)\Longleftrightarrow U(2,1,1,1).
\]
Concretely, every representation
\[
n=x^2+2y^2+z^3+w^4
\]
would yield, simply by exchanging \(x\) and \(y\), the representation
\[
n=2y^2+x^2+z^3+w^4
\]
for the second quadruple, and conversely.

On the other hand, the proposed list treats these two quadruples differently. The quadruple
\[
(1,2,1,1)
\]
is explicitly the first quadruple in the list, whereas
\[
(2,1,1,1)
\]
does not occur in it. To see the latter directly from the displayed finite list, the entries having fourth coordinate \(1\) are precisely
\[
\begin{aligned}
 &(1,2,1,1),\ (1,3,1,1),\ (1,6,1,1),\ (2,3,1,1),\ (2,4,1,1),\\
 &(1,1,2,1),\ (1,4,2,1),\ (1,2,3,1),\ (1,2,4,1),\ (1,2,12,1).
\end{aligned}
\]
None of these is \((2,1,1,1)\), and every remaining entry in the proposed list has fourth coordinate different from \(1\). Hence \((2,1,1,1)\) is not in the list.

Suppose, for contradiction, that the conjectured classification were true. It would then apply to every positive quadruple and assert
\[
U(a,b,c,d)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
(a,b,c,d)\text{ belongs to the proposed list}.
\]
All four coordinates of \((1,2,1,1)\) are positive. Since this quadruple belongs to the list, the right-to-left direction of the conjectured equivalence would imply
\[
U(1,2,1,1).
\]
By the square-variable symmetry, it would follow that
\[
U(2,1,1,1).
\]
All four coordinates of \((2,1,1,1)\) are also positive, so the left-to-right direction of the conjectured equivalence, now applied to this second quadruple, would force
\[
(2,1,1,1)
\]
to belong to the proposed list. But the explicit inspection above shows that it does not. This is a contradiction.

Therefore the stated “if and only if” classification is false. Notice that this disproof does not require separately deciding whether \((1,2,1,1)\) actually represents every natural number. The two swapped quadruples necessarily have exactly the same representability behavior, while the proposed classification assigns them different list-membership behavior; consequently no biconditional between those two properties can hold for both quadruples.
